findings.message: In non-interactive mode (CI), creating an iOS destination with API-key auth always fails, and each attempt first uploads the user's Apple .p8 private key to the server, where it is left unattached. The options schema (lines 16-34) has appleApiKeyFile and appleIssuerId but no appleApiKeyId option. appleApiKeyId is only a local, `let appleApiKeyId: string | undefined;` (line 53), so it is always undefined. With `--apple-api-key-file X --apple-issuer-id Y` and no TTY, authMethod becomes 'apiKey' (line 193). Lines 233-240 then call `appAppleApiKeysService.create(...)`, and line 242 `if (!appleApiKeyId) { if (!isInteractive()) { consola.error('You must provide the Apple API Key ID...'); process.exit(1); } }` exits. There is no flag that can supply the value. The command's own non-interactive error message (line 212) tells users that passing --apple-api-key-file and --apple-issuer-id is enough, which it is not.

`apps:destinations:get` and `apps:destinations:list` may print the Apple app-specific password to stdout and CI logs, because they dump the whole destination object unfiltered. The DTO declares the secret as a returned field: src/types/app-destination.ts:10 `appleAppPassword: string | null;`. get.ts:74 `console.log(JSON.stringify(destination, null, 2))` and :76 `console.table(destination)`, and list.ts:39/41, print every field with no redaction. If the API returns what the type says, the password is shown in plain text.

Certificate passwords, key passwords and the Apple app-specific password are prompted with a plain text prompt, so they echo on screen and stay in terminal scrollback and session recordings. certificates/create.ts:119 `prompt('Enter the certificate password:', { type: 'text' })`, :139 `prompt('Enter the key password (leave empty if none):', { type: 'text' })`, and destinations/create.ts:296 `prompt('Enter the App-specific password:', { type: 'text' })`. package.json already depends on @clack/prompts 0.7.0, which provides a masked password prompt.

Service-account and API private keys are uploaded before the remaining inputs are collected and before the destination is created, so any later cancel, missing input or API error leaves the uploaded key on the server with no cleanup and no ID shown. Android: `appGoogleServiceAccountKeysService.create(...)` (line 182) runs before `appDestinationsService.create(...)` (line ~318). iOS: `appAppleApiKeysService.create(...)` (line 235) runs before the Key ID, Issuer ID and Team ID prompts (lines 242-315). Each of those prompts can `process.exit(1)` or be cancelled; prompt() calls process.exit(0) on cancel. No delete call exists in either key service, and the key IDs are never printed.

Provisioning profiles are uploaded before the certificate exists. A failed certificate upload (for example a wrong password) leaves the profiles orphaned, and a failed link step leaves a created certificate without its profiles, so a retry makes a duplicate. Lines 160-169 loop over `appProvisioningProfilesService.create(...)`. Then `appCertificatesService.create(...)` runs at line 172, then `updateMany(...)` at line 186. Nothing is rolled back if a later step throws. A wrong second --provisioning-profile path also throws from `fs.readFileSync(profilePath)` (line 161) after the first profile is uploaded. CreateAppProvisioningProfileDto already has a `certificateId` field (src/types/app-provisioning-profile.ts:16) that the service sends, which would let the profiles be uploaded after the certificate, but the field is never used.

The only non-interactive way to pass certificate, key and Apple passwords is as command-line flags, which expose them in shell history and process listings. certificates/create.ts:19,21 (`keyPassword`, `password`), certificates/update.ts (same options) and destinations/create.ts:23 / update.ts:19 (`appleAppPassword: z.string().optional()`) are plain flags. No environment-variable or file input exists, unlike the existing `apps:environments:set`, which offers `--secret-file` (src/commands/apps/environments/set.ts:26).

An unrequested change to the shared app picker hard-codes a 50-app limit with no paging. In every interactive command, apps after the first 50 may become impossible to select. `let apps = await appsService.findAll({ organizationId, limit: 50 });` sits in promptAppSelection, which most commands use. The re-fetch after creating an app (line 57, `appsService.findAll({ organizationId })`) has no limit, so the two calls disagree. No certificate or destination code needs this change.

Certificate, profile and key files are read with fs.readFileSync and no existence check. A mistyped path gives a raw ENOENT error, which in production is also reported to Sentry along with the local path. certificates/create.ts:154,161 and destinations/create.ts:180,233 call `fs.readFileSync(...)` directly. Existing commands check first with `fileExistsAtPath` and print a clear error (e.g. liveupdates/register.ts:193-196, 214-222). src/index.ts captureException skips only ZliError, ZodError and AxiosError, so the fs Error is sent to Sentry.

Delete by name removes the first server match without checking that it is exact or unique, and the confirmation prompt never names what will be deleted. A loose or duplicate name match may delete the wrong signing certificate or destination, and the delete cannot be undone. `const certificates = await appCertificatesService.findAll({ appId, name, platform }); ... certificateId = firstCertificate.id;` (lines 37-43), followed by `prompt('Are you sure you want to delete this certificate?')` (line 74), which shows no name or ID. destinations/delete.ts uses the same pattern. With --yes or no TTY, no confirmation is shown at all.

In interactive mode, a `--name` given without `--platform` is silently ignored, so the user gets an unfiltered picker instead of the certificate or destination they named. The name filter applies only when `name && platform` (line 36). Otherwise the interactive branch prompts for a platform and calls `findAll({ appId, platform })` (line 56) without `name`. The same happens in certificates/get.ts, destinations/delete.ts and destinations/get.ts.

`apps:destinations:update` takes raw server key IDs (`--apple-api-key-id`-style IDs for uploaded keys and Google service-account keys), but no command uploads a replacement key or prints a key ID, so rotating a destination's credentials through the CLI is not possible. update.ts options include `appAppleApiKeyId` and `appGoogleServiceAccountKeyId` as plain strings. destinations/create.ts uploads keys internally (lines 182, 235) and prints only `Destination ID` (line ~335). The key services expose only `create`, with no command wired to them.

iOS and Android certificates must have a non-empty password. That may reject valid .p12 or keystore files exported without one, and non-interactive runs cannot proceed at all. `if (!password && (platform === 'android' || platform === 'ios')) { if (!isInteractive()) { ...exit(1) } password = await prompt(...); if (!password) { consola.error('You must provide a certificate password.'); process.exit(1); } }` (lines 114-124). The service sends the password only `if (dto.password)`, so the API side treats it as optional.

The `--yes` flag says it skips confirmation prompts, but this command has none. What it actually does is silently skip the key-password and provisioning-profile inputs, which can create an incomplete certificate. `yes: z.boolean().optional().describe('Skip confirmation prompts.')` (line 34). It is used only at line 138 (`!options.yes` gating the key-password prompt) and line 145 (gating the provisioning-profile prompt).
